subject: ss-paediatric-gastroenterology
title: Paediatric Gastroenterology
examPattern: NBEMS NEET-SS Paediatric Group. 150 questions (100 questions in 2024+ format). Feeder: MD/DNB Paediatrics. All questions are feeder-speciality content covering General Paediatrics and all Paediatric Super-Specialities.
books: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Vol 2, Part XVIII (The Digestive System, Chapters 350-380)

sections.title: Esophageal, Gastric and Upper GI Disorders

lessonTopics.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux and Reflux Disease in Infants and Children

mustKnow.fact: Physiologic gastroesophageal regurgitation in healthy infants peaks at 4 months of age (affecting over 50% of infants) and resolves spontaneously by 12-14 months.
GERD is defined when reflux of gastric contents leads to troublesome symptoms or complications such as failure to thrive, esophagitis, or respiratory symptoms.
First-line non-pharmacological management includes thickened feeds, smaller frequent feedings, and maintaining upright posture after feeding; prone sleep is contraindicated due to SIDS risk.
A 2 to 4 week trial of maternal dairy elimination in breastfed infants or extensively hydrolyzed formula in formula-fed infants is recommended before starting acid suppression.
Sandifer syndrome is characterized by paroxysmal dystonic neck extension and head cocking associated with feeding, mimicking neurological spasms but representing a protective anti-reflux posture.
When acid suppression is indicated for erosive esophagitis, omeprazole or esomeprazole (1 mg/kg/day) is administered for a 4 to 8 week course.
Multichannel intraluminal impedance combined with pH monitoring (MII-pH) is the gold standard investigation to quantify both acidic (pH < 4) and non-acidic reflux episodes.
Routine use of metoclopramide or domperidone is not recommended in pediatric GERD due to unacceptable central nervous system extrapyramidal effects and QT prolongation.

lessonTopics.title: Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Diagnosis and Multimodality Therapy

mustKnow.fact: Eosinophilic esophagitis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field (HPF) on esophageal mucosal biopsy (peak count x400 magnification) in the absence of secondary causes.
Endoscopic signs include circular rings (trachealization / felinization), linear longitudinal furrows, white plaques or exudates, mucosal fragility (crepe-paper esophagus), and strictures.
At least 6 mucosal biopsies from both proximal/mid and distal esophagus are required to achieve diagnostic sensitivity exceeding 95-97%.
High-dose PPI therapy (omeprazole 1-2 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 8-12 weeks) achieves histological remission in 30-50% of patients through anti-eotaxin-3 and acid-blocking mechanisms.
Swallowed viscous budesonide slurry (1 mg daily for < 10 yr, 2 mg daily for >= 10 yr) or fluticasone inhaler sprayed into the mouth and swallowed provides effective topical mucosal immunosuppression.
Empirical six-food elimination diet (SFED) eliminates cow milk, wheat, egg, soy, peanuts/tree nuts, and fish/shellfish, achieving clinical and histological remission in over 70% of children.
Dupilumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting interleukin-4 receptor alpha (IL-4R-alpha) inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, is approved for pediatric patients aged 1 year and older weighing >= 15 kg.
Acute food bolus impaction in older children and adolescents is caused by eosinophilic esophagitis in over 50% of presenting emergency cases.

lessonTopics.title: Helicobacter pylori Infection and Peptic Ulcer Disease in Children

mustKnow.fact: Testing for H. pylori in children is indicated only during investigation of endoscopically confirmed peptic ulcer disease; screening in functional abdominal pain is strictly advised against.
Diagnosis requires either positive bacterial culture from gastric biopsy OR histopathology showing gastritis with H. pylori plus at least one other biopsy-based test (rapid urease test or PCR).
Stool antigen test (monoclonal ELISA) and 13C-urea breath test are validated for confirming eradication at least 4-8 weeks after antibiotic completion, but serology is unreliable.
First-line eradication therapy consists of high-dose PPI (amoxicillin + clarithromycin OR amoxicillin + metronidazole) administered for a full 14 days.
If local clarithromycin resistance exceeds 15% or susceptibility testing is unavailable, clarithromycin is replaced by metronidazole or bismuth-based quadruple therapy.
Quadruple therapy includes high-dose PPI, bismuth subsalicylate (8 mg/kg/day), metronidazole (20 mg/kg/day), and amoxicillin (50 mg/kg/day) or tetracycline (in children > 8 years).

Primary peptic ulcers in children are predominantly duodenal, chronic, and H. pylori-associated; secondary ulcers are gastric, acute, and triggered by critical illness, burn injury (Curling ulcer), or head trauma (Cushing ulcer).
Pediatric gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma is strongly driven by H. pylori and frequently regresses completely following successful bacterial eradication alone.

lessonTopics.title: Caustic Ingestion and Esophageal Foreign Bodies

mustKnow.fact: Esophageal button battery impaction is a surgical emergency; electrical current generation and alkaline hydroxide production cause liquefactive necrosis and aortic perforation within 2 hours.
Early oral administration of honey or sucralfate (10 mL every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses) before hospital arrival acts as a physical barrier and neutralizes localized alkalinity.

mustKnow.term: Timing of endoscopy in caustic injury
mustKnow.fact: Diagnostic upper endoscopy for caustic chemical ingestion is ideally performed within 12 to 24 hours and avoided after 48 hours to minimize perforation risk in friable tissue.
Zargar classification predicts stricture risk: Grade 1 (edema/erythema), Grade 2a (superficial ulceration), Grade 2b (circumferential deep ulceration, > 70% stricture risk), Grade 3 (necrosis).
Corticosteroids do not prevent esophageal stricture formation following caustic ingestion and increase the risk of systemic infection and perforation.
Ingestion of multiple magnets or a magnet plus ferromagnetic metallic foreign body carries high risk of bowel entrapment, pressure necrosis, fistula, and perforation, requiring urgent extraction.
An esophageal coin in an asymptomatic child can be observed for 12-24 hours if unwitnessed; persistent presence beyond 24 hours requires endoscopic removal.

Pediatric achalasia features incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis on high-resolution manometry (bird beak sign on barium swallow), treated with laparoscopic Heller myotomy or POEM.

modules.title: Celiac Disease and Small Bowel Enteropathies

lessonTopics.title: Celiac Disease: ESPGHAN Guidelines and No-Biopsy Approach

mustKnow.fact: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (anti-tTG IgA) combined with total serum IgA is the mandatory first-line screening investigation for suspected celiac disease.
In selective IgA deficiency (total IgA < 0.2 g/L), IgG-based tests (deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or anti-tTG IgG) must be used.

Under ESPGHAN 2020 guidelines, if anti-tTG IgA is >= 10 times upper limit of normal (ULN), a biopsy-free diagnosis is established if endomysial antibodies (EMA-IgA) are positive on a second, separate blood draw.
HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 testing has high negative predictive value (> 99%) but is no longer required for the non-biopsy diagnostic pathway under 2020 criteria.
Duodenal biopsy histology shows Marsh 1 (intraepithelial lymphocytosis > 25/100 enterocytes), Marsh 2 (crypt hyperplasia), and Marsh 3 (villous atrophy: 3a partial, 3b subtotal, 3c total).
Celiac disease prevalence is increased in type 1 diabetes (5-10%), Down syndrome (5-12%), Turner syndrome, Williams syndrome, and autoimmune thyroiditis.
Safe daily dietary gluten threshold in celiac disease is strictly under 10-20 parts per million (ppm) or < 10-20 mg/day.

Celiac crisis is a life-threatening presentation in young infants featuring severe hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, metabolic acidosis, and profuse secretory diarrhea, requiring systemic corticosteroids.

lessonTopics.title: Short Bowel Syndrome and Intestinal Failure in Children

mustKnow.fact: Pediatric short bowel syndrome results from surgical resection leaving remnant small bowel length < 25% of expected for gestational age, or < 30-50 cm without ileocecal valve (< 15-20 cm with valve).
Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC, 35-40%), intestinal atresia, midgut volvulus, and gastroschisis are the leading causes of pediatric intestinal failure.
Preservation of the ileocecal valve prevents retrograde colonic bacterial colonization into the small bowel and slows transit time to double mucosal fluid absorption.
The ileum possesses unique capacity for mucosal hyperplasia and structural adaptation, as well as exclusive receptor-mediated absorption of vitamin B12 and conjugated bile acids.
IFALD (PNAC) is driven by lack of enteral stimulation, continuous intravenous soybean-based lipid emulsions, recurrent central line sepsis, and phytosterols.
Substituting pure soybean lipid emulsions with fish-oil-based lipid emulsion (Omegaven) reverses cholestasis in IFALD due to high omega-3 fatty acids and alpha-tocopherol.
Teduglutide, a recombinant glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) analogue, stimulates crypt cell proliferation and villus hypertrophy to reduce parenteral nutrition volume requirements.
Serial Transverse Enteroplasty (STEP) and Longitudinal Intestinal Lengthening and Tailoring (LILT / Bianchi) expand mucosal absorptive surface in dilated bowel loops.

lessonTopics.title: Protein-Losing Enteropathy and Congenital Diarrheal Disorders

mustKnow.fact: Fecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance exceeding 27 mL/24 hr (or random spot fecal concentration > 54 mg/dL) confirms protein-losing enteropathy due to its resistance to enteric degradation.
Waldmann disease is characterized by congenital malformation of intestinal lymphatics leading to diffuse lymph leakage, hypoproteinemia, lymphopenia, and hypogammaglobulinemia.
Strict low-fat diet supplemented with Medium-Chain Triglycerides (MCT) is the cornerstone therapy because MCTs are absorbed directly into the portal venous circulation, bypassing lymphatics.
PLE develops in 3-10% of post-Fontan single-ventricle patients due to elevated systemic venous pressure and mesenteric lymphangiectasia, treated with oral budesonide or sildenafil.

Congenital chloride diarrhea (SLC26A3 mutation) presents in utero with polyhydramnios and maternal ultrasound showing dilated fluid-filled bowel, featuring fecal chloride > 90 mmol/L exceeding the sum of fecal sodium and potassium.
Congenital sodium diarrhea (NHE3 or SPINT2 mutations) features massive watery secretory diarrhea with alkaline stools and high fecal sodium (> 100 mmol/L).
MYO5B gene mutations cause microvillus inclusion disease, with enterocyte brush border atrophy and pathognomonic cytoplasmic microvillus inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.
EPCAM gene mutations cause congenital tufting enteropathy (intestinal epithelial dysplasia), characterized by focal crowding of enterocytes forming teardrop-shaped epithelial tufts on biopsy.

lessonTopics.title: Cow Milk Protein Allergy, FPIES and Allergic Proctocolitis

mustKnow.fact: Cow milk protein allergy encompasses IgE-mediated reactions (urticaria, anaphylaxis within 2 hours) and non-IgE-mediated gastrointestinal syndromes (FPIES, FPIAP, enteropathy).
FPIAP presents in breastfed infants aged 2-8 weeks with visible blood and mucus streaks in stool despite normal growth and happy, thriving demeanor.
Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES) causes profuse repetitive emesis 1-4 hours post-ingestion leading to dehydration, hypothermia, methemoglobinemia, and hypovolemic shock.
Extensively hydrolyzed formula (eHF) is the first-line therapeutic formula for mild-to-moderate CMPA in formula-fed infants, reserving amino acid formula (AAF) for severe disease or anaphylaxis.
In exclusively breastfed infants with suspected CMPA, maternal strict exclusion of all dairy products with calcium supplementation (1000 mg/day) is maintained.
Soy infant formula is not recommended under 6 months of age due to phytate content, isoflavone phytoestrogens, and concomitant cross-reactivity in up to 10-15%.
Tolerance develops in over 50% of CMPA children by 1 year of age and exceeds 80-90% by 3-5 years, reassessed via supervised oral food challenge at 6-12 month intervals.
Children who tolerate baked milk (muffins, cookies where heat denatures conformational epitopes) develop resolution of unheated milk allergy significantly faster.

lessonTopics.title: Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Meckel Diverticulum and Polyps

mustKnow.fact: Meckel diverticulum rule of 2s: occurs in 2% of population, located within 2 feet of ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, contains 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric 60%, pancreatic 5%), presents around 2 years of age.
Ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa from ectopic gastric acid secretion produces classic sudden, painless, massive rectal bleeding (brick-red or maroon stool).
Meckel scan using 99mTc-pertechnetate is selectively taken up by ectopic gastric parietal cells, with sensitivity enhanced by H2-blockers (cimetidine/ranitidine), glucagon, and pentagastrin.
Juvenile hamartomatous polyps are the most common GI polyps in children (> 80%), predominantly solitary, pedunculated, located in the rectosigmoid, presenting with painless hematochezia.
JPS is an autosomal dominant condition (SMAD4 or BMPR1A mutations) defined by >= 5 juvenile polyps in colorectum, polyps throughout GI tract, or any juvenile polyps with family history.
STK11/LKB1 mutation causes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, featuring mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation around mouth/digits and small bowel hamartomatous polyps prone to intussusception.

APC gene mutation causes FAP with hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps; 100% colorectal cancer risk mandates screening sigmoidoscopy from age 10-12 and prophylactic colectomy in late adolescence.
Cowden and Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndromes feature macrocephaly, lipomas, penile freckling, and mixed GI polyposis associated with germline PTEN mutations.

modules.title: Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease and VEO-IBD

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Crohn Disease: Paris Classification and Mucosal Healing

mustKnow.fact: Paris pediatric classification defines age of onset as A1a (< 10 years), A1b (10-17 years), and A2 (17-40 years).
Impaired linear growth velocity and delayed puberty precede gastrointestinal symptoms in up to 25-30% of children with Crohn disease, classified as G1 (growth delay).
Fecal calprotectin > 250 mcg/g indicates active mucosal inflammation, whereas values < 100-250 mcg/g correlate with endoscopic mucosal healing.

Exclusive Enteral Nutrition (EEN) using exclusive polymeric or elemental formula for 6 to 8 weeks is first-line induction therapy for pediatric luminal Crohn disease, achieving 80% remission without steroid toxicity.
Infliximab (5 mg/kg at 0, 2, and 6 weeks, then maintenance every 8 weeks) is first-line for high-risk disease: deep extensive ulcerations, perianal fistulae, or severe growth retardation.
Maintenance infliximab trough levels should be maintained between 5 and 10 mcg/mL to achieve and sustain endoscopic mucosal healing.
Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and NUDT15 genotype/phenotype testing is mandatory prior to starting azathioprine (2-2.5 mg/kg/day) to prevent fatal myelosuppression.
Non-caseating epithelioid granulomas on mucosal biopsy confirm Crohn disease, found in 40-60% of pediatric patients, frequently in upper GI or normal-appearing mucosa.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Ulcerative Colitis and Acute Severe Colitis

mustKnow.fact: Pediatric Ulcerative Colitis Activity Index (PUCAI): < 10 indicates remission; 10-34 mild; 35-64 moderate; and >= 65 defines acute severe colitis.
Extensive colitis or pancolitis (E4 by Paris classification) occurs in over 60-80% of pediatric patients with ulcerative colitis at presentation, far higher than in adults.
Oral 5-aminosalicylate (mesalazine) at 60-80 mg/kg/day (maximum 4.8 g/day) combined with topical rectal 5-ASA (25 mg/kg/day) is first-line induction and maintenance.
Patients with PUCAI >= 65 require immediate hospitalisation, abdominal radiography, and intravenous methylprednisolone at 1-1.5 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg/day) in 2 divided doses.
PUCAI score > 45 on Day 3 of IV steroids predicts steroid failure; PUCAI >= 65 on Day 5 mandates second-line rescue therapy with infliximab (5-10 mg/kg) or intravenous ciclosporin.
Toxic megacolon is defined as non-obstructive transverse colon dilatation > 56 mm in children over 10 years (or > 40 mm in younger children) accompanied by systemic toxicity.
Screening colonoscopy with chromoendoscopy is initiated 8-10 years post-diagnosis in pediatric pancolitis, or immediately at diagnosis if coexisting Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis is present.
Restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA / J-pouch) is the curative surgical treatment of choice for medically refractory disease or dysplasia.

lessonTopics.title: Very Early Onset IBD (VEO-IBD) and Monogenic Enteropathies

mustKnow.fact: Very Early Onset IBD is defined as diagnosis under 6 years of age, with infantile IBD under 2 years and neonatal IBD under 28 days of life.
Loss-of-function mutations in IL10, IL10RA, or IL10RB cause hyperinflammatory, severe penetrative infantile colitis with perianal fistulae, highly resistant to anti-TNF therapy.

mustKnow.term: Curative HSCT in IL-10 receptor defect
mustKnow.fact: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is curative for IL-10 and IL-10 receptor deficiency, resolving intestinal and perianal disease completely.
IPEX (Immunodysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked) is caused by FOXP3 mutations leading to regulatory T-cell deficiency, presenting with enteropathy, type 1 diabetes, and eczema.
X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis (XIAP) deficiency causes refractory Crohn-like colitis, severe perianal disease, and high susceptibility to hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).
Comprehensive targeted gene panel or whole-exome sequencing is mandatory in all children presenting with IBD under 6 years of age prior to biologic escalation.
TTC7A mutations cause multiple intestinal atresia and severe combined immunodeficiency with apoptotic enterocolitis; HSCT corrects immunodeficiency but does not cure the epithelial defect.
CYBB or NCF gene mutations causing CGD feature Crohn-like colitis in 30-40% of patients; treatment requires caution because anti-TNF therapy significantly increases fatal fungal infection risks.

sections.title: Lower GI Emergencies, Motility and Functional Disorders

lessonTopics.title: Hirschsprung Disease: Aganglionosis and Enterocolitis

mustKnow.fact: Hirschsprung disease is characterized by complete absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses due to premature arrest of neural crest craniocaudal migration.
Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life occurs in over 90% of affected term neonates.
Short-segment aganglionosis (confined to rectosigmoid) accounts for 75-80% of cases and exhibits a 4:1 male preponderance; long-segment accounts for 15-20%.

Full-mucosal or rectal suction biopsy taken at least 2 cm above the dentate line is the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating absence of ganglion cells and prominent nerve trunk hypertrophy (> 40 mcm).
Absence of calretinin-positive mucosal nerve fibers in the lamina propria has a sensitivity and specificity exceeding 99% for diagnosing aganglionosis.
HAEC presents with explosive foul-smelling diarrhea, abdominal distension, and septic shock; immediate rectal washouts with warm saline and broad-spectrum antibiotics are life-saving.
Contrast enema demonstrates a distinct cone-shaped transition zone between the narrowed, tonically contracted aganglionic segment and the dilated proximal normal colon.
Definitive surgical correction utilizes transanal endorectal pull-through (Soave), Duhamel retrorectal pull-through, or Swenson procedure to resect aganglionic bowel.

lessonTopics.title: Intussusception: Clinical Triad, Ultrasound and Enema Reduction

mustKnow.fact: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants between 3 months and 3 years, with peak incidence between 5 and 9 months.
Over 90% of cases in infants under 2 years are idiopathic ileocolic intussusception triggered by viral gastroenteritis or adenovirus-induced lymphoid hyperplasia.
Children older than 2-3 years frequently have a pathological lead point: Meckel diverticulum (most common), intestinal duplication cyst, polyp, or Burkitt lymphoma.
The classic triad of episodic crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and red currant jelly stools is present in under 30-40% of cases at initial presentation.
Abdominal ultrasonography has near 100% sensitivity, showing the pathognomonic target or doughnut sign (3-5 cm diameter) in transverse view and pseudokidney sign in longitudinal view.
Air enema (pneumatic reduction) has an 85-90% success rate with lower radiation dose than hydrostatic barium reduction, controlled at maximum pressure of 120 mmHg in infants.
Evidence of peritonitis, pneumoperitoneum (intestinal perforation), or hemodynamic shock constitutes an absolute contraindication to non-operative reduction.
Intussusception recurs in approximately 10% of cases following successful air enema reduction, with over half of recurrences occurring within the first 48-72 hours.

lessonTopics.title: Functional Constipation and Rome IV Criteria

mustKnow.fact: Rome IV functional constipation requires at least 2 criteria for 1 month in infants or 2 months in older children: <= 2 stools/week, painful/hard stools, history of withholding, large fecal mass in rectum, or retentive fecal incontinence.
Stool withholding behavior typically emerges during toilet training or after painful defecation, where the child crosses legs, tightens gluteals, and rocks back and forth to resist urge.
Polyethylene glycol (PEG 3350) is the first-line laxative for both fecal disimpaction (1-1.5 g/kg/day for 3-6 days) and maintenance therapy (0.4-0.8 g/kg/day).
Maintenance laxative therapy must be continued for at least 2 months and not discontinued until the child achieves regular bowel movements without pain for at least 1 month.
Retentive encopresis represents involuntary soiling from overflow of liquid stool around a hard, impacted chronic fecaloma, mistaken for true diarrhea.

Red flags mandating investigation for organic causes: delayed meconium passage > 48 hours, sacral dimple with hair tuft, abnormal anal position, absent anal wink, or empty rectum with explosive stool on exam.
Presence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) upon rectal balloon inflation conclusively excludes Hirschsprung disease without requiring rectal biopsy.
Recommended daily dietary fiber intake in children older than 2 years is calculated as age in years plus 5 g/day (or 10 g per 1000 kcal).

lessonTopics.title: Clostridioides difficile and Chronic Infectious Diarrhea

mustKnow.fact: C. difficile colonization occurs in up to 30-70% of healthy infants under 12 months without clinical illness; testing is strongly discouraged in infants < 1 year.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics (clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, amoxicillin-clavulanate) disrupt intestinal microbiota, predisposing to toxigenic C. difficile colitis.
Diagnostic algorithm combines glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen screen with sensitive enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for toxins A and B, or nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT/PCR).
Oral vancomycin (40 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses, max 500 mg/day) or fidaxomicin (for age >= 6 months) for 10 days is first-line; metronidazole is reserved only when vancomycin is unavailable.
Sigmoidoscopy demonstrates raised, discrete, yellowish-white plaques on erythematous colonic mucosa representing pseudomembranes composed of fibrin, mucin, and neutrophils.
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is recommended for children with recurrent C. difficile infection failing at least two antibiotic courses, achieving > 85-90% cure.

Giardiasis causes chronic malabsorptive diarrhea with foul, floating stools and secondary lactase deficiency, diagnosed by stool antigen ELISA and treated with metronidazole (15-30 mg/kg/day for 5-7 days) or tinidazole.
Cryptosporidium parvum causes severe, protracted watery diarrhea in immunocompromised children (HIV, CD40L deficiency), treated with nitazoxanide alongside immune reconstitution.

modules.title: Pancreatitis, Cystic Fibrosis and Biliary Atresia

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis

mustKnow.fact: Pediatric acute pancreatitis requires at least 2 of 3 criteria: abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin, serum lipase or amylase >= 3 times upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging findings.
Serum lipase remains elevated longer (8-14 days vs 3-5 days for amylase) and provides significantly higher sensitivity (over 90%) and specificity in children.
Biliary disease (20-30%), medications (valproate, asparaginase, 6-mercaptopurine, steroids; 15-25%), blunt abdominal trauma (handlebar injury; 10-15%), and systemic infection are primary triggers.
Early enteral feeding within 24-48 hours (oral low-fat or nasogastric/nasojejunal) is superior to bowel rest, reducing length of stay and systemic inflammatory response.
Targeted crystalloid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance volume during the initial 24 hours prevents hypoperfusion and pancreatic necrosis.
Recurrent and chronic pancreatitis in children is driven by mutations in PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen, autosomal dominant), SPINK1, CFTR, and CTRC.
A pancreatic pseudocyst is a fibrous non-epithelialised fluid collection developing at least 4 weeks following acute necrotizing pancreatitis.
Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TPIAT) is indicated for intractable pain in chronic pancreatitis refractory to medical and endoscopic therapy.

lessonTopics.title: Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency and Cystic Fibrosis GI Manifestations

mustKnow.fact: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency occurs in approximately 85% of cystic fibrosis patients, particularly those homozygous for the severe class II mutation F508del.
Fecal elastase-1 concentration < 200 mcg/g stool indicates pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, with < 100 mcg/g defining severe insufficiency; not affected by exogenous enzyme therapy.

Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) is dosed to lipase units: 500-1000 units/kg/meal (infants: 2000-4000 units per 120 mL feed), capped strictly below 2500 units/kg/meal or 10,000 units/kg/day.
Excessive PERT dosing exceeding 10,000 units of lipase/kg/day leads to fibrosing colonopathy, characterized by longitudinal colonic strictures and severe mural thickening.
Deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) mandate daily supplementation in water-miscible form with regular annual serum monitoring.
Meconium ileus presents in 15-20% of CF neonates with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and microcolon on gastrografin contrast enema.
DIOS is unique to CF, presenting with ileocecal fecal obstruction treated with oral PEG 3350 or meglumine diatrizoate (Gastrografin) enemas.
Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor triple therapy significantly improves intestinal pH and weight Z-scores, though pancreatic insufficiency is rarely reversed once extensive fibrosis is established.

lessonTopics.title: Biliary Atresia and Choledochal Malformations

mustKnow.fact: Biliary atresia is a progressive fibro-obliterative destruction of the extrahepatic biliary tree, affecting 1 in 10,000 to 15,000 live births (higher in East Asians).
High-resolution ultrasound demonstrates the triangular cord sign (echogenic fibrous band > 4 mm at the anterior wall of the right portal vein bifurcation) with > 95% specificity.
Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scintigraphy after 5 days of oral phenobarbital priming (5 mg/kg/day) demonstrates prompt hepatic uptake but zero bowel excretion at 24 hours.
Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy achieves the highest bile drainage rate (> 70-80%) when performed before 45-60 days of life, declining rapidly if delayed beyond 90 days.
Prophylactic oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or neomycin and ursodeoxycholic acid (15-20 mg/kg/day) are administered post-Kasai to prevent ascending bacterial cholangitis.

Todani classification divides choledochal cysts: Type I (fusiform CBD dilatation, 80-85%), Type II (diverticulum), Type III (choledochocele), Type IV (multiple intra/extrahepatic), Type V (Caroli disease).
APBJ features a common channel > 5 mm outside the duodenal wall, allowing reflux of pancreatic enzymes into the biliary tree leading to cyst formation and malignant degeneration.
Choledochal cysts carry a lifetime cholangiocarcinoma risk of 10-30%, mandating complete cyst excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy rather than simple drainage.

sections.title: Hepatology, Metabolic Liver Disease and Transplantation

modules.title: Neonatal Cholestasis, Metabolic Liver Disease and Cirrhosis

lessonTopics.title: Evaluation of Neonatal Cholestasis and Alagille Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: Direct/conjugated bilirubin > 1.0 mg/dL (17 mcmol/L) regardless of total bilirubin (or direct > 20% of total if total bilirubin exceeds 5.0 mg/dL) mandates urgent workup.
Infant stool color card screening programs identify persistent pale acholic stools to prompt evaluation for biliary atresia before 30-45 days of age.
Alagille syndrome is an autosomal dominant multi-organ disorder caused by mutations in JAG1 (94-96%) or NOTCH2 (1-2%), encoding Notch signaling ligands.
Liver biopsy in Alagille syndrome shows a bile duct to portal tract ratio < 0.4 (normal is 0.9 to 1.8), defining ductal paucity.
Clinical criteria include chronic cholestasis, butterfly vertebrae on spine radiographs, posterior embryotoxon on slit-lamp examination, peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, and triangular facies.
Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis (PFIC) types 1 (ATP8B1) and 2 (ABCB11/BSEP) have characteristically normal or low serum GGT, whereas PFIC 3 (ABCB4/MDR3) has markedly elevated GGT.
Odevixibat, an oral inhibitor of the ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT), reduces serum bile acids and pruritus in patients with PFIC aged 3 months and older.

All cholestatic infants require high-dose fat-soluble vitamin supplementation: Vitamin A (5,000-10,000 IU/day), D (calcitriol 0.05-0.2 mcg/kg/day), E (TPGS 15-25 IU/kg/day), and K1 (2.5-5 mg 2-7 times/week).

lessonTopics.title: Wilson Disease and Metabolic Liver Diseases in Children

mustKnow.fact: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive copper storage disorder caused by mutations in ATP7B on chromosome 13q14, disrupting biliary excretion and ceruloplasmin incorporation.

The Leipzig / Ferenci score incorporates Kayser-Fleischer rings, neurologic symptoms, low serum ceruloplasmin, Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, liver copper, urinary copper, and ATP7B mutations (score >= 4 establishes diagnosis).
Copper deposition in the Descemet membrane of the cornea produces Kayser-Fleischer rings, present in over 95% of neurological cases but in only 50% of children with hepatic presentation.
Baseline 24-hour urinary copper excretion > 100 mcg/day (or > 40 mcg/day in children) is diagnostic; following D-penicillamine challenge test, excretion > 1,600 mcg/day confirms disease.
Hepatic parenchymal copper concentration on liver biopsy exceeding 250 mcg/g dry weight (or 4 mcmol/g) is the diagnostic gold standard.
D-penicillamine (20 mg/kg/day in 2-3 divided doses) or trientine (20 mg/kg/day) acts as initial chelating agent, accompanied by pyridoxine (vitamin B6 25-50 mg/day) to prevent deficiency.
Oral elemental zinc (50 mg two or three times daily) induces intestinal mucosal enterocyte metallothionein synthesis to block dietary copper absorption during maintenance.

Fulminant Wilson presentation features Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, marked hyperbilirubinemia with normal/low alkaline phosphatase (alk phos to total bilirubin ratio < 2.0), requiring emergency liver transplantation.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Autoimmune Hepatitis and Sclerosing Cholangitis

mustKnow.fact: Type 1 AIH is characterized by positive Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA) and/or Anti-Smooth Muscle Antibodies (ASMA / actin) and elevated serum immunoglobulin G (IgG).

Type 2 AIH is characterized by Anti-Liver-Kidney Microsomal type 1 (anti-LKM1) and/or Anti-Liver Cytosol type 1 (anti-LC1) antibodies, typically presenting in infants and young girls with aggressive course.

The simplified IAPG criteria allocate points for autoantibody titers (>= 1:40 in children = 1 pt; >= 1:80 = 2 pts), elevated IgG, compatible histology (interface hepatitis), and absence of viral hepatitis.
Liver biopsy characteristically demonstrates interface hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates crossing the limiting plate and rosetting of hepatocytes.
Prednisolone or prednisone at 1.5-2 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg/day) tapered over 4-8 weeks is first-line induction, achieving biochemical remission in over 80-90% of children.
Azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg/day) is added after 2-4 weeks to enable steroid sparing and maintain long-term remission, requiring 6-thioguanine nucleotide (6-TGN) monitoring.

Autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis (ASC) coexists in up to 50% of pediatric AIH patients, displaying features of AIH on biopsy but characteristic bile duct beading on magnetic resonance cholangiography (MRCP).

Immunosuppressive therapy must be maintained for at least 2 to 3 years of complete biochemical remission (normal transaminases and normal IgG) before considering a repeat biopsy and trial off therapy.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation

mustKnow.fact: Pediatric acute liver failure requires: biochemical evidence of acute liver injury, no known chronic liver disease, and coagulopathy uncorrected by parenteral vitamin K (PT-INR >= 1.5 with encephalopathy OR PT-INR >= 2.0 without encephalopathy).

Hepatic encephalopathy is subtle and notoriously difficult to detect in infants and non-verbal children, presenting as irritability, disrupted sleep cycles, or inconsolable crying rather than asterixis.

Intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion (150 mg/kg loading over 1 hr, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hr, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hr) is life-saving in paracetamol toxicity and improves transplant-free survival in non-paracetamol PALF.

Cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension threaten when arterial ammonia exceeds 150-200 mcmol/L, managed with 3% hypertonic saline (target sodium 145-150 mmol/L) and neuroprotective head-up 30 degrees positioning.
Pediatric End-Stage Liver Disease (PELD) score calculates waiting list mortality risk in children < 12 years using serum bilirubin, INR, albumin, growth failure (< -2 SD), and age < 1 year.
Split-liver transplantation divides an adult deceased donor liver into a left lateral segment (segments II and III) for an infant and an extended right trisegment for an adult recipient.
Calcineurin inhibitor tacrolimus (target trough 8-12 ng/mL early, 5-8 ng/mL late) combined with mycophenolate mofetil and corticosteroids forms standard post-transplant immunosuppression.
PTLD is a life-threatening complication driven by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) proliferation in immunosuppressed graft recipients, treated with reduced immunosuppression and rituximab.

lessonTopics.title: Extrahepatic Portal Vein Obstruction and Pediatric Portal Hypertension

mustKnow.term: EHPVO as leading cause in children
mustKnow.fact: Extrahepatic portal vein obstruction (EHPVO) with cavernous transformation of the portal vein is the most common cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and upper GI bleeding in children in developing nations.
History of neonatal umbilical vein catheterization or neonatal omphalitis/sepsis is identified as the precipitating thrombosis etiology in 30-50% of EHPVO patients.

Children with EHPVO present with massive hematemesis and huge splenomegaly with hypersplenism (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia) but completely normal hepatic synthetic function (normal albumin, INR, and transaminases).

Vasoactive infusion with octreotide (1-2 mcg/kg IV bolus followed by 1-2 mcg/kg/hr continuous infusion) or terlipressin effectively lowers splanchnic blood flow and controls acute variceal hemorrhage.
Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the primary endoscopic treatment of choice for esophageal varices in children, carrying fewer strictures and ulcerations than endoscopic sclerotherapy.

Meso-Rex bypass (mesenterico-left portal vein bypass using internal jugular vein autograft) is the physiological surgical cure for EHPVO, restoring physiological hepatopetal flow and reversing hypersplenism.

Extensive pericholedochal venous collaterals in long-standing EHPVO compress and deform the extrahepatic bile ducts (portal biliopathy / cavernoma cholangiopathy), causing secondary cholestasis and biliary stones.
Propranolol titrated to reduce resting heart rate by 20-25% is used for secondary variceal prophylaxis in older children, though EVL is generally preferred in younger children.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD)

mustKnow.fact: MASLD (formerly NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease in children, affecting over 35-40% of children with obesity.
Screening is recommended in all children with obesity from age 9-11 using serum ALT: abnormal thresholds are > 26 U/L in boys and > 22 U/L in girls (nearly half of adult upper limits).
Pediatric MASLD frequently manifests as Type 2 NASH: prominent panacinar steatosis, periportal inflammation, and periportal fibrosis without ballooning degeneration or Mallory-Denk bodies.
The I148M variant in the patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing 3 (PNPLA3) gene strongly predisposes to severe hepatic steatosis, MASH progression, and fibrosis in Hispanic and Asian youth.
Dietary elimination of sugar-sweetened beverages, reduction of free fructose, and moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise >= 60 minutes/day achieving 5-10% weight loss is the primary proven treatment.
Oral vitamin E (RRR-alpha-tocopherol 400-800 IU/day) significantly reduces hepatocyte ballooning and steatosis in non-diabetic children with biopsy-proven MASH (TONIC trial).
Vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) measures liver stiffness in kilopascals (kPa), with values > 7-9 kPa indicating significant fibrosis requiring specialist evaluation.
Pediatric MASH can progress aggressively to cryptogenic cirrhosis and end-stage liver failure in early adulthood, requiring liver transplantation.
